title: PaneFlip: zones for your Mac
desc: PaneFlip is a free, open-source macOS menu-bar app. Split your Mac's screens into zones. Drop apps into them.
hero.lead: Split your Mac's screens into zones. Drop apps into them.
hero.note: Free and open source (MIT). Needs macOS 27.
how.sub: Three ideas, and your windows always know where to go.
how.1p: Drag a window while you hold <kbd>⌘</kbd>. The zones light up; let go over one and the window slides in and fills it. Apps you put in a zone are remembered and return when they reopen.
how.2p: Several apps can share one zone. Click the zone in the island, then an app, or use the arrow keys to flip.
how.3p: A layout can go on past the edge of the display, with as many screens as you like. Scroll over the island in the menu bar, or hold the keys and scroll with two fingers.
feat.h2: Made for the way you work
feat.sub: Layouts you draw, windows that stack, and a Mac that remembers.
snap.h3: Drag a window into a zone
snap.p: Hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> while you drag and the zones light up. Let go over one and the window slides in and fills it. PaneFlip remembers which app belongs where and puts it back when the app reopens.
stack.p: Put more apps in a zone and they stack. Click the zone in the island, then an app, or use the arrow keys to flip. The next window glides in beside the one it replaces.
scroll.p: Hold <kbd>⌥</kbd> <kbd>⌃</kbd> and scroll with two fingers: the windows follow your fingers, pass several at once and settle on the nearest one. A mouse wheel steps one window at a time. The speed is a setting.
beyond.p: A layout can go on past the edge of the display, with as many screens as you like. Scroll over the island in the menu bar, or hold <kbd>⌘</kbd> <kbd>⌥</kbd> <kbd>⌃</kbd> and scroll, and the whole layout slides over.
editor.p: Click to split a zone, drag a line to resize, drag a zone onto its neighbour to merge. Or start from one of twenty common shapes. Name your layouts and zones, and set a gap for each.
layouts.p: Every desktop of a display can use the layout you choose for it. Pick another from the menu bar and the windows glide to their new zones.
more.sub: The details that make it feel like part of the Mac.
more.1a: Draw zones in the editor: click to split, drag a line to resize, drop one on a neighbour to merge.
more.1b: Start from twenty common shapes or a blank layout. Name layouts and zones, set a gap per layout.
more.1c: Switch layouts from the menu bar. Every desktop of a display can use its own.
more.2b: Choose which app opens in which zone and open them all with one click.
more.2c: A window dragged out of its zone glides back to the size it had.
more.3a: Any number of screens past each edge, one after the other.
more.3b: Hold keys and scroll with two fingers or the mouse wheel; a window that gets focus brings its zone into view.
more.4a: Several displays and desktops. Unplug a display and its apps move to the main screen; plug it in and they go back.
more.4b: Closed, hidden and minimized windows leave their zone and return when they do.
more.4c: Updates from inside the app. 46 languages.
sc.sub: Every one of them can be changed in Settings.
sc.1a: Snap a window into a zone
sc.3a: Next / previous window of the zone
sc.4a: Screens beyond the right / left edge
sc.6a: Scroll toward the screens beyond the edge
inst.sub: PaneFlip asks for two permissions on the first launch, Accessibility and Screen Recording, and tells you why.
inst.1p: Open the .dmg of the latest release and drag PaneFlip into Applications. The app is signed with its own certificate, not an Apple developer one: the first time, open it, then choose System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Open Anyway.
inst.2p: Homebrew removes the quarantine mark, so no extra step is needed.
inst.2q: Or take the quarantine mark off by hand:
